content: Paracoccidioidomycosis, also referred to as Lutz-Splendore-Almeida disease or Brazilian blastomycosis, is a fungal infection caused by the thermally dimorphic fungi Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and Paracoccidioides lutzii. Despite being colloquially called South American blastomycosis, it is caused by a different fungal species than the one responsible for blastomycosis. This infection is highly prevalent in South and Central America. The natural habitat of the causative fungi remains uncertain, but it is hypothesized to be aquatic. Histopathological examination of infected tissue reveals the fungus in its yeast form, characterized by a distinctive pilot's wheel appearance due to its multiple budding structures. The discovery of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis dates back to 1908, when it was first identified by Brazilian physician Adolfo Lutz. In 1912, Luigi Splendore, another Brazilian physician, renamed the organism Zimonema brasiliense. Subsequently, in 1930, Floriano de Almeida established the genus Paracoccidioides to distinguish it from other fungal species, such as Coccidioides immitis. Paracoccidioidomycosis can be classified into several forms based on clinical presentation and disease progression. According to Franco et al. (1987), the classifications include: paracoccidioidomycosis infection, paracoccidioidomycosis disease, paracoccidioidomycosis associated with immunosuppression, and the residual form (sequelae). The disease itself can be further categorized based on symptom duration into acute, subacute, or chronic forms. The chronic form is subdivided into unifocal (affecting a single organ or site) and multifocal (involving multiple organs or systems). The primary mode of transmission is through the inhalation of fungal spores, which are believed to originate from soil in endemic rural areas. The acute form of paracoccidioidomycosis must be differentiated from conditions such as lymphoma, leukemia, toxoplasmosis, and sarcoidosis. The chronic form, on the other hand, can mimic diseases such as tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis, actinomycosis, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, squamous cell carcinoma, and Wegener's granulomatosis. Paracoccidioidomycosis is endemic to South and Central America, with the highest prevalence observed among agricultural workers in countries such as Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela. Brazil accounts for the majority of reported cases. The disease predominantly affects men, although the infection itself can occur in individuals of any gender. This gender disparity is thought to be influenced by hormonal factors, as estrogen may inhibit fungal growth. Several risk factors contribute to the development of paracoccidioidomycosis, including poor hygiene, malnutrition, smoking, and excessive alcohol consumption. In endemic areas, children are often exposed to the fungus but typically do not develop the disease until later in life. The disease may remain latent for years before manifesting clinically, often in adulthood.
